questions.q: How much work is done by an ideal gas in an isochoric process (at constant volume)?
questions.hint: The work done by the gas is expressed by $A = \int P dV$. What happens to $dV$ if $V = \text{constant}$?
explanations: Correct! In an isochoric process, the volume does not change ($\Delta V = 0$), so the expansion/compression work is $A = P \Delta V = 0$.
Incorrect. The work would be proportional to pressure if there were a change in volume, but here $\Delta V = 0$.
Incorrect. In isochoric heating, temperature changes the internal energy of the gas ($\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$), not the work.

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of an ideal gas during its adiabatic compression?
questions.hint: Use the first law of thermodynamics: $\Delta U = Q + A_{ext}$. With $Q = 0$, the work done on the gas increases its internal energy.
options: The temperature of the gas increases
The temperature of the gas decreases
The temperature of the gas remains constant
explanations: Correct! Since $Q = 0$, compression work is done on the gas ($A_{ext} > 0$), increasing its internal energy $\Delta U > 0$ and therefore its temperature.
Incorrect. The temperature would decrease during an adiabatic expansion, when the gas does work against external forces.
Incorrect. The temperature remains constant only in an isothermal process.

questions.q: What is the primary cause of ocean tides on Earth?
questions.hint: Tides are caused by the gravitational attraction of nearby celestial bodies.
options: The gravitational attraction of the Sun and the Moon
Only the gravitational attraction of the Moon
The centrifugal force generated by the daily rotation of Earth
explanations: Correct! Tides are caused by the combined gravitational (tidal) effect of the Moon and the Sun.
Incorrect. The Moon has the primary influence, but the Sun also makes a significant contribution (about 46% of the Moon's).
Incorrect. Earth's rotation affects the periodicity of the tides, but tidal forces themselves are created by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun.

questions.q: A ball bounces up and down on a table without losing energy, reaching a height of $19.6\text{ m}$. Is this simple harmonic motion, and what is its period? (Assume $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.hint: Simple harmonic motion requires a restoring force proportional to displacement ($F = -kx$). The period is equal to the total time of ascent and descent.
options: No, it is not simple harmonic motion; the period is $4\text{ s}$
Yes, it is simple harmonic motion; the period is $4\text{ s}$
No, it is not simple harmonic motion; the period is $2\text{ s}$
explanations: Correct! The gravitational force has a constant magnitude and is not proportional to displacement, so the motion is not simple harmonic. The fall time is $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = 2\text{ s}$, and the complete period (ascent and descent) is $T = 4\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. The motion is not simple harmonic because the gravitational force $mg = \text{constant}$, and is not proportional to $x$.
Incorrect. $2\text{ s}$ is the duration of motion in a single direction (fall or ascent).

questions.q: On a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, a ball is thrown vertically upward and caught at the same height after $6$ seconds. What were the initial velocity and maximum height reached by the ball?
questions.hint: The time of ascent is half the total time ($t_{ascent} = 3\text{ s}$). The velocity is $v_0 = g t_{ascent}$, and the height is $h = \frac{g t_{ascent}^2}{2}$.
explanations: Correct! $t_{ascent} = 3\text{ s}$. Initial velocity $v_0 = 10 \cdot 3 = 30\text{ m/s}$. Height $h = \frac{10 \cdot 3^2}{2} = 45\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. A similar result would be obtained using the total time of $6\text{ s}$ instead of the ascent time of $3\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. When calculating the height, it is necessary to divide $g t^2$ by 2.

questions.topic: Motion on an Inclined Plane with Friction
questions.q: A body slides from rest down a smooth inclined plane at an angle of $30^\circ$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). After traveling $2.5\text{ m}$, it enters a horizontal section with a coefficient of friction $\mu = 0.5$. After how many seconds will the body stop?
questions.hint: Find the acceleration on the plane ($a_1 = g \sin 30^\circ$), the velocity at the end of the descent ($v = \sqrt{2 a_1 s}$), and then the braking time ($t = v / (\mu g)$).
explanations: Correct! $a_1 = 10 \cdot 0.5 = 5\text{ m/s}^2$. At the end of the descent $v = \sqrt{2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2.5} = 5\text{ m/s}$. The deceleration due to friction is $a_{fric} = 0.5 \cdot 10 = 5\text{ m/s}^2$. Time $t = 5 / 5 = 1\text{ s}$.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the braking acceleration or the velocity at the end of the descent.
Incorrect. You forgot to consider that the acceleration on the inclined plane depends on the sine of the angle.

questions.q: Two $30\,\Omega$ resistors are connected in parallel to a $90\text{ V}$ power supply. What current flows from the supply and what is the voltage across each resistor?
questions.hint: In a parallel connection of identical resistors, $R_{eq} = R/2$, and the voltage across each is equal to that of the supply.
explanations: Correct! $R_{eq} = 15\,\Omega$. Current $I = 90 / 15 = 6\text{ A}$. In a parallel connection, voltage is equal across all branches ($90\text{ V}$).
Incorrect. The voltage is halved in a series connection, not a parallel one.
Incorrect. $1.5\text{ A}$ is the current that would flow through resistors connected in series.

questions.q: A light bulb operates from a $12\text{ V}$ source with a current of $0.2\text{ A}$. How much energy (in Joules) is dissipated as heat during $1$ hour of operation?
questions.hint: Convert time to seconds ($1\text{ hour} = 3600\text{ s}$) and apply the formula $Q = U I t$.
explanations: Correct! Energy $Q = U \cdot I \cdot t = 12 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 3600 = 8640\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $2.4\text{ W}$ is the power of the bulb $P = UI$, not the energy dissipated in an hour.
Incorrect. You forgot to convert hours into seconds and multiplied the power by 60 minutes instead of 3600 seconds.

questions.q: Two resistors $R_1 = 10\,\Omega$ and $R_2 = 20\,\Omega$ are connected in series to a $120\text{ V}$ source. What is the current in the circuit, and what are the voltage drops across $R_1$ and $R_2$?
questions.hint: Add the resistances to find the total current: $I = U / (R_1 + R_2)$. Then find $U_1 = I R_1$ and $U_2 = I R_2$.
explanations: Correct! $R_{tot} = 10 + 20 = 30\,\Omega$. Current $I = 120 / 30 = 4\text{ A}$. Voltages: $U_1 = 4 \cdot 10 = 40\text{ V}$, $U_2 = 4 \cdot 20 = 80\text{ V}$.
Incorrect. Such a current would be obtained in a parallel connection, where the voltage across both resistors is the same.
Incorrect. Voltage divides in proportion to resistances, not into equal parts.

questions.q: Between two parallel conductors $1\text{ m}$ long, located at a distance of $0.1\text{ m}$ from each other, currents of $10\text{ A}$ flow in the same direction. What are the nature and order of magnitude of the interaction force?
questions.hint: Currents in the same direction attract each other. Force $F = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\pi r} = \frac{2 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 1}{0.1}$.
options: They attract each other; order of magnitude of the force is $10^{-4}\text{ N}$
They repel each other; order of magnitude of the force is $10^{-4}\text{ N}$
They attract each other; order of magnitude of the force is $10^{-2}\text{ N}$
explanations: Correct! Currents in the same direction attract each other. The force is $F = 2 \cdot 10^{-4}\text{ N}$, corresponding to an order of magnitude of $10^{-4}\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. Conductors carrying parallel currents in the same direction attract, they do not repel.
Incorrect. Error of two orders of magnitude in calculating distance or the magnetic constant.

questions.q: What is the flux of the electric field intensity vector through a closed surface enclosing a single neutral hydrogen atom?
questions.hint: Recall the total electric charge of a neutral atom (proton + electron).
options: It is proportional to the electron charge
It depends on the atomic radius
explanations: Correct! A neutral atom has a net charge $Q_{int} = q_p + q_e = 0$, so by Gauss's law, the electric flux is zero.
Incorrect. The electron's charge is balanced by the proton's charge in the nucleus.
Incorrect. Flux is determined solely by the total charge inside the surface, not by the size of the atom.

questions.topic: Work of Forces and Work-Energy Theorem
questions.q: A body of mass $10\text{ kg}$ rises vertically upward from rest on Earth with constant acceleration, reaching a speed of $10\text{ m/s}$ in $5\text{ seconds}$. How much work (in Joules) was done? (Assume $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$).
questions.hint: Find acceleration $a = v/t$, height $h = \frac{a t^2}{2}$, lifting force $F = m(g+a)$, and work $A = F \cdot h$.
explanations: Correct! $a = 10/5 = 2\text{ m/s}^2$. Height $h = 2 \cdot 25 / 2 = 25\text{ m}$. Force $F = 10(9.8 + 2) = 118\text{ N}$. Work $A = 118 \cdot 25 = 2950\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $500\text{ J}$ is only the increase in kinetic energy, without considering the gain in potential energy.
Incorrect. $2450\text{ J}$ is only the work against gravity ($mgh$), without accounting for the acceleration of the body.

questions.q: What is the electric field flux through a closed surface created by a charge $Q$ located OUTSIDE that surface?
questions.hint: All field lines from the external charge entering the closed surface also exit from the opposite side.
options: It is strictly equal to zero
explanations: Correct! According to Gauss's law, flux is determined only by internal charges. External charges yield a net flux of zero through a closed surface.
Incorrect. $Q / \varepsilon_0$ would be the flux if the charge $Q$ were located inside the closed surface.
Incorrect. The factor of 2 does not appear in Gauss's law.

questions.q: If magnetic monopoles (magnetic charges) existed in nature, what would the magnetic field flux through a closed surface be equal to?
questions.hint: Analogy with Gauss's law for electric charge.
options: It would be proportional to the total magnetic charge inside the surface
It would still always be equal to zero
It would be proportional to the electric current passing through the surface
explanations: Correct! By analogy with electrostatics, the existence of magnetic charges would make the flux $\oint \vec{B} d\vec{S}$ proportional to the magnetic charge enclosed within.
Incorrect. Zero flux is precisely caused by the absence of magnetic monopoles in our universe.
Incorrect. Electric current is proportional to the line integral (circulation) of the magnetic field, not its flux through a closed surface.

questions.topic: Electric Field of a Charged Sphere
questions.q: A charged conducting sphere has a negative charge $-Q$. How is the electric field intensity vector directed in outer space?
questions.hint: Electric field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges.
options: Radially toward the center of the sphere
Radially away from the center of the sphere
Tangentially to the surface of the sphere
explanations: Correct! The field of a negative charge is directed toward the charge itself, i.e., toward the center of the conducting sphere.
Incorrect. Direction radially outward corresponds to a positively charged sphere.
Incorrect. Field intensity on the surface of a conductor is always perpendicular to it (radial).

questions.q: How many Joules of work must be done to charge a capacitor of capacitance $0.5\text{ F}$ to a potential difference of $20\text{ V}$?
questions.hint: Use the formula $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$.
explanations: Correct! $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0.5 \cdot 20^2 = 0.25 \cdot 400 = 100\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. You forgot to divide by 2 in the energy formula ($C V^2 = 200$).
Incorrect. $10$ is obtained by mistakenly multiplying $C \cdot V$ without squaring the voltage.

questions.q: Which parameter does the pressure of a liquid at the bottom of a container NOT depend on?
questions.hint: Hydrostatic pressure formula: $P = \rho g h$. Pay attention to the shape of the container.
options: On the shape of the container and the area of its bottom
On the height of the liquid column $h$
On the density of the liquid $\rho$
explanations: Correct! This phenomenon is known as the hydrostatic paradox: pressure depends only on height $h$ and density $\rho$, but not on the shape or volume of the vessel.
Incorrect. The height of the liquid column $h$ directly determines hydrostatic pressure.
Incorrect. Pressure is directly proportional to the density of the liquid.

questions.q: An inverted bucket containing a volume of air $V$ at sea level is submerged to a depth of $40\text{ m}$. What will happen to the volume of air at this depth?
questions.hint: Every $10\text{ m}$ of depth increases hydrostatic pressure by $1\text{ atm}$. Total pressure $P = P_{atm} + P_{hydro}$.
options: It will decrease and become approximately $V/5$
It will decrease and become approximately $V/4$
explanations: Correct! At a depth of $40\text{ m}$, the hydrostatic pressure is $4\text{ atm}$. Total pressure is $1 + 4 = 5\text{ atm}$. By Boyle's Law, the volume will decrease by a factor of 5 ($V/5$).
Incorrect. $V/4$ would be obtained without accounting for the external atmospheric pressure of $1\text{ atm}$ at the surface.
Incorrect. Gases are compressible, so as pressure increases, volume decreases.

questions.q: A wheel rotates with an angular velocity $\omega = \frac{\pi}{5}\text{ rad/s}$. How many revolutions will it make in $1$ minute?
questions.hint: Find the rotation frequency per second $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}$, then multiply by $60\text{ seconds}$.
explanations: Correct! $f = \frac{\pi/5}{2\pi} = 0.1\text{ rev/s}$. In one minute ($60\text{ s}$), the wheel will complete $0.1 \cdot 60 = 6\text{ revolutions}$.
Incorrect. You forgot to divide by 2 when converting radians to full revolutions.
Incorrect. $60$ would be obtained with a frequency of $1\text{ rev/s}$.

questions.q: A bullet of mass $20\text{ g}$, flying at a speed of $800\text{ m/s}$, embeds itself in a wooden block of mass $380\text{ g}$. What is the velocity of the block with the bullet after impact?
questions.hint: Use the formula for inelastic collision: $m_1 v_1 = (m_1 + m_2) v$.
explanations: Incorrect. Error in summing the masses of the system.
Incorrect. This value is obtained by mistakenly dividing momentum by the mass of the block alone without the bullet.

questions.q: A transformer has $100$ turns in the primary winding and $300$ turns in the secondary winding. If the secondary voltage is $270\text{ V}$, what is the primary voltage?
questions.hint: Transformation formula: $U_1 / U_2 = N_1 / N_2$.
explanations: Correct! $U_1 = U_2 \cdot \frac{N_1}{N_2} = 270 \cdot \frac{100}{300} = 90\text{ V}$.
Incorrect. $810\text{ V}$ would be obtained by incorrectly multiplying the voltage by the turns ratio, treating a step-up transformer as step-down.
Incorrect. Error in calculating the turns ratio.

questions.q: An incompressible fluid flows at a velocity of $2\text{ m/s}$ in a pipe with a cross-sectional area of $12\text{ cm}^2$. What is its velocity when the pipe narrows to $3\text{ cm}^2$?
questions.hint: Use the continuity equation: $S_1 v_1 = S_2 v_2$.
explanations: Correct! $v_2 = \frac{S_1 v_1}{S_2} = \frac{12 \cdot 2}{3} = 8\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Direct proportionality error instead of inverse.
Incorrect. Simple difference of areas used instead of their ratio.

questions.topic: Dynamics of a System of Particles
questions.q: If the vector sum of external forces acting on a system of particles is zero ($\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$), select the CORRECT statement:
questions.hint: Consequence of Newton's first law for a system of point masses and its center of mass.
options: The center of mass of the system moves with constant velocity in a straight line
All particles in the system move with constant velocity in a straight line
The angular momentum of the system relative to any point is conserved
explanations: Correct! The center-of-mass motion theorem states that if $\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0$, the acceleration of the center of mass is zero, meaning it moves in uniform linear motion.
Incorrect. Internal forces can cause individual particles to rotate or accelerate relative to each other.
Incorrect. For conservation of angular momentum, the total torque of external forces must be zero, not just the net force.

questions.q: How does the Coulomb force of interaction between two point charges change if the distance between them is increased by 3 times?
questions.hint: Coulomb's force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance: $F \sim 1/r^2$.
explanations: Correct! Increasing distance $r$ by 3 times decreases the force by $3^2 = 9$ times.
Incorrect. Force depends on the square of distance, not the linear distance.
Incorrect. Increasing distance decreases interaction force, not increases it.

questions.q: A spring with stiffness $200\text{ N/m}$ stretches by $2\text{ cm}$ under an applied force. What is the magnitude of the elastic force?
questions.hint: Formula $F = k \Delta x$. Do not forget to convert centimeters to meters ($2\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m}$).
explanations: Correct! $F = 200 \cdot 0.02 = 4\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. Error caused by failing to convert centimeters to meters ($200 \cdot 2$).
Incorrect. An order-of-magnitude error in unit conversion.

questions.q: How does the oscillation period of a simple pendulum change if the length of the string is increased by 4 times?
questions.hint: Formula for the period of a simple pendulum: $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$.
explanations: Correct! The period is proportional to the square root of length $\sqrt{l}$. Increasing $l$ by 4 times increases period $T$ by $\sqrt{4} = 2$ times.
Incorrect. You forgot to take the square root of the change in length.
Incorrect. Increasing length increases oscillation period, not decreases it.

questions.q: A gas is supplied with $500\text{ J}$ of heat, and simultaneously does $200\text{ J}$ of work. By how much did the internal energy of the gas change?
questions.hint: First law of thermodynamics: $Q = \Delta U + A \implies \Delta U = Q - A$.
explanations: Correct! $\Delta U = Q - A = 500 - 200 = 300\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $700\text{ J}$ is obtained by mistakenly adding heat and work.
Incorrect. Internal energy increased because supplied heat exceeds work done by the gas.

questions.q: What happens to the perceived frequency of a sound when the sound source approaches a stationary observer?
questions.hint: As the source approaches, wave fronts are 'compressed', decreasing the distance between crests.
explanations: Correct! As the source approaches, the observer hears a higher frequency (a higher pitch).
Incorrect. Frequency decreases when the source moves away from the observer.
Incorrect. Frequency would remain constant if source and observer were at rest relative to each other.

questions.q: A light ray passes from air into glass with a refractive index $n = 1.5$. How does the propagation speed of light change?
questions.hint: Refractive index is related to speed by $n = c / v$.
explanations: Correct! The speed of light in the medium is $v = c / n$. Entering a denser medium ($n = 1.5$), speed decreases by $1.5$ times.
Incorrect. In a medium with $n > 1$, light speed is always lower than in a vacuum.
Incorrect. Speed of light changes when passing from one medium to another.

questions.q: A sound wave with a frequency of $500\text{ Hz}$ propagates at a speed of $340\text{ m/s}$. What is the wavelength of this wave?
questions.hint: Relationship between speed, frequency, and wavelength: $v = \lambda f \implies \lambda = v / f$.
explanations: Correct! $\lambda = 340 / 500 = 0.68\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $1.47$ is obtained by mistakenly dividing frequency by speed ($f / v$).
Incorrect. $170\text{ km}$ would be obtained by multiplying speed and frequency.
